_README: Per-author title exclusions for fetch_textgrid.py, applied as case-insensitive
regexes against the object title. The Digitale Bibliothek reproduces public-domain
editions WITHOUT flagging whether the text is the author's own: third-party-edited
editions, unauthorised editions and the author's adaptations of other writers all
appear under his name. For authorship verification that is not a metadata nuisance
but a contaminated identity label, so any author with a complicated publication
history needs auditing before his texts enter a bank.
Each entry records WHY, because the exclusion has to be defensible in the paper.

audit_finding: Italian; reaches the Digitale Bibliothek in German translation. The GND
provenance gate cannot see this -- neither the edition records nor an exact
name search return a usable authority record -- so the exclusion is recorded
here by hand rather than guessed at automatically. Same reasoning as
shakespeare_william: the grammatical habit of a translated text is the
translator's.
Italian, German translation, no decisive GND record -- see
petrarca_francesco.
Excluded ENTIRELY, and the reason generalises. The want-list matched him
because our German drama bank holds him for German productions, and the
Digitale Bibliothek then supplied two things, both wrong for us: the ENGLISH
originals (1.1M words, caught by the language test in looks_german), and the
Schlegel-Tieck GERMAN TRANSLATION (553k drama + 21k verse), which passes any
language test because it is genuinely German.
The translation is the more dangerous of the two. Its grammatical habit is the
translator's, and Ludwig Tieck is one of our own three-genre authors -- so
keeping it would place one hand in the bank under two identities and
manufacture a same-author signal across what we would score as different
authors.
GENERAL RULE: a foreign author reached through a translation is never usable
for authorship verification, whatever the language test says.
Audited 2026-09-07 against the 200 objects listed for May. The disputed
material is confined to one collection ('Collection 101': the Fischer-Ausgabe
Waldroeschen volumes, Die Liebe des Ulanen, Deutsche Herzen, Der Weg zum Glueck,
Scepter und Hammer, Die Juweleninsel) and ALL 48 of its objects are aggregation
manifests that yield no TEI body, so none of that text entered the harvest.
The rules below therefore cost only ~168k words of genuinely fetched material
(Der Waldlaeufer, Der Waldkoenig, riddles, open letters) out of 5.34M, and stand
as a guard in case those aggregations are ever resolved to their leaf chapters.
What remains is 'Collection 58' -- the Fehsenfeld Reiseerzaehlungen and the
Erzgebirgische Dorfgeschichten -- which is May's own text.
why: Fischer-Ausgabe (1902-03): an edition published AGAINST May's will, whose text
was edited on the publisher's behalf by Paul Staberow. Waldroeschen was issued in
it as six volumes -- Die Tochter des Granden / Der Schatz der Mixtekas / Matavese,
der Fuerst des Felsens / Erkaempftes Glueck I-III -- so those titles denote an
Muenchmeyer colportage novels (1882-87): authorship disputed. May claimed the
objectionable passages were interpolated by other hands; the manuscripts are lost
so it cannot be settled, and modern scholarship (Harder) leans towards most of the
text being May's own. Excluded as a precaution, not as a verdict -- the safe
choice for a method paper is to drop a disputed text and say so.
Der Waldlaeufer: May's reworking of Gabriel Ferry's 'Le Coureur des Bois' via
Gustav Fuellner's German translation, so its sentence structure descends from a
translator, which is exactly what a grammatical-habit method measures.
Non-narrative material: riddles, proverb collections and occasional prose are not
running text and would enter the stream as a different register.
